A B S T R A C T
Effective metro stations evacuation in the event of a fire is a crucial component of ensuring safe
metro operations. To achieve efficient metro fire simulation and evacuation optimization in high-
density and complex metro station environments, a hybrid approach that integrates building
information modeling (BIM), fire dynamics simulator (FDS) and multiobjective optimization al­
gorithm is proposed. A BIM model of a metro station was imported into Pyrosim software for
smoke simulation and Pathfinder for evacuation. An orthogonal design yielded data for hybrid
algorithm optimization to seek effective evacuation measures. The applicability of this approach
is verified by taking a metro station as an example. The results indicate that:(1) The proposed
method can effectively simulate metro station fire and realize evacuation optimization. (2) The
predictive model combined with machine learning performs well, among which the prediction
accuracy of Bayesian optimization (BO) natural gradient boosting (NGBoost) is above 0.85, better
than random forest (RF) and adaptive boosting (AdaBoost). SHapley Additive explanation (SHAP)
is used to unveil that passenger flow and the number of exits are the most important factors in
evacuation. (3) Under the premise of meeting the maximum passenger flow, the optimized
evacuation objectives have been significantly improved, with improvements in evacuation time,
evacuation density, and cost optimization by 31.02 %, 2.70 % and 51.41 %, respectively, and the
overall improvement is 28.38 %. Hence, the proposed method can provide decision-making tools
for developing effective evacuation optimization plans, while fully considering the complexity
and multi-objective problems of evacuation events.

1. Introduction
The metro, as an efficient, safe, and environmentally friendly urban public transportation tool, has gained significant attention [1].
The normal operation of the urban metro system has made an important contribution to the sustainable development of transportation.
However, as a large number of metros are put into operation, the number of interruptions in metro operations and accidents have
increased significantly, which unfortunately include catastrophic events, which have a significant impact on the metro system [2,3]. As
one type of massive system engineering project, the metro system are exposed to various artificial and natural disasters during its
operational period [4]. Due to the complexity of the internal environment of urban metro systems and the uncertainty of the external
environment, the manifestations of disasters during the systems’ operational period are diverse. Previous studies have considered fires
to be one of the main types of disasters in metro system [5,6]. The metro station is situated in a confined and narrow space with high
density of personnel and equipment. Once fire happened, the evacuation and escape of individuals would be severely restricted.
Therefore, effective evacuation in metro stations is a crucial aspect in ensuring the safe metro operations, as well as an important part
of the sustainable development of metro operating system.
The metro, as a unique type of underground transportation system, experiences high passenger flow and dense populations, leading
to the consequences of metro fires often severe. In addition, the interior of the metro is often decorated with combustible materials,
which can lead to rapid fire spread. In specific, the combustion of certain modern materials can produce toxic gases, increasing the
hazards of such accidents [7,8]. Recently, metro fires have occurred more frequently and damagingly, such as the one in Daegu, South
Korea on February 18, 2003 [9], and the metro fire accident in Hong Kong, China in February 2017 [10] and so on, resulting in
significant casualties and property damage [11]. In these accidents, toxic gases produced by fires can shorten the time required for safe
evacuation and cause irreversible harm to human beings. Therefore, it is necessary to achieve effective evacuation of personnel as
quickly as possible in the event of a fire [12]. Traditional methods for studying metro stations fire simulation and personnel evacuation
include experimental testing, formula calculations, and computer simulation modeling [13,14].
However, the methods mentioned above have significant limitations. For experimental testing, while real-world scenario data offer
high reliability, the approach suffers from prohibitive costs, limited experimental scenarios, and difficulties in replicating extreme
conditions [15]. Regarding theoretical formulas, simplification assumptions often lead to failures in multi-factor coupling, with strong
parameter dependency and delayed theoretical advancements [16]. Although traditional fire and evacuation simulation software has
long been developed, most simulation software fails to model complex operations and generates inadequate model accuracy. It is
time-consuming and tedious to model large transfer stations, which often leads to inaccurate simulation results due to imprecise
modeling. As a result, it becomes challenging to meet the demands of subsequent simulation needs [17]. Therefore, a method
combining Building Information Modeling (BIM) technology with traditional computer simulation software is proposed in this
research. This approach not only meets the requirements for rapid and accurate modeling of transfer stations but also integrates
comprehensive model information involved in subsequent fire and evacuation scenarios [18,19]. Some scholars at home and abroad
have applied BIM technology on metro fire evacuation [20,21]. For instance, Sun and Turkan integrated BIM, FDS, and Agent-Based
Modeling (ABM) to develop an automated simulation model, which is used to simulate evacuation behaviors and investigate the
available safe evacuation time (ASET) during evacuation incidents [22]。Li et al. employed BIM technology and lightweight digital
twin technology to simulate complex fire evacuation scenarios in metro stations. This approach enabled real-time, dynamic visuali­
zation of smoke propagation and crowd behavior, thereby enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of fire evacuation simulations [23]。
The application of BIM technology has enhanced the visualization level of fire evacuation simulation in metro stations.
With the development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, AI algorithm has been applied to the studies of metro fire evac­
uation, though few researches are found [13,24,25]. Chen et al. introduced a novel fire monitoring system that integrates wireless
sensor networks, edge computing, multi-source data fusion, and deep neural networks. This system employs Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM) neural networks for time-series prediction of sensor data and then utilizes Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) to fuse multi-source
data for identifying fire risks [26]. Li et al. combined the social force model with deep learning, taking into account two
often-overlooked issues in crowd evacuation: pedestrian tracking and individual differences. This integration resulted in a novel
pedestrian detection method that simulated the evacuation process during subway fires, offering a fresh perspective on personnel
evacuation in metro stations [27]. The above-mentioned artificial intelligence technologies have enhanced the intelligent level of fire
evacuation in metro stations. However, the above methods only take into account the single objective of personnel evacuation and lack

optimization for multiple objectives (such as evacuation time and evacuation density). Notably, the evacuation events in metro sta­
tions are complex and affected by numerous factors. The high level of uncertainty in the problem-solving process often presents
significant challenges in finding the optimal solutions, as well as lacking of interpretability. Thus, it is worth conducting in-depth
research on how to consider multiple factors in metro station fire simulation and evacuation, in order to achieve improved pre­
dictions of the evacuation process and evacuation management.
To address the above issue, this study aims (1) to identify the key factors that affect the evacuation performance of metro stations;
(2) to unveil the complex relationship between evacuation objectives and influencing factors in metro station fires, as well as enhance
the transparency of the model; (3) to conduct multi-objective optimization renovation for fire evacuation in metro stations to achieve
effective evacuation. In order to achieve the above objectives, a hybrid method that integrates BIM, FDS and multi-objectives opti­
mization algorithm approach is proposed. This investigation approach can represent the complex relationship between desired
evacuation objectives and their influencing factors to achieve effective evacuation in metro station fire scenarios. The novelties of this
study are as follow: (a) integrating BIM models, FDS techniques and multi-objectives optimization algorithm to enhance the intelligent
level of metro fire evacuation simulation and optimization; (b) using the simulation results of different fire scenarios, to determine the
evacuation objectives and influential factors in fire situations, and obtain their nonlinear mapping relationships via machine learning
algorithms and SHAP is used to enhance the interpretability of the model; (c) utilising a hybrid intelligent optimization algorithm to
achieve multi-objective optimization of evacuation objectives and paths in the event of a fire, aiming to enhance the efficiency of metro
station evacuations. The investigation approach proposed will contribute to improving the evacuation paths for personnel in metro
station fire scenarios.
The structure of this paper is as follows. Section 2 reviews the related works about the simulation and evacuation of metro stations
fire. Section 3 proposes a hybrid framework that integrates BIM, FDS and intelligent optimization algorithms approach with detailed
step-by-step procedures. In Section 4, the applicability and effectiveness of the proposed method are proved by taking a metro station
in China as an example. Section 5 discusses the influence of smoke on evacuation optimization and suggests the improvement mea­
sures. Section 6 gives the summary of this research and future works.
2. Related work
The study of personnel evacuation behavior in response to metro fire emergencies often relies on computer simulation and data
statistics. Lan et al. [28] noted that the research on personnel safety evacuation behavior cannot ignore the study of personnel reactions
in emergency accidents. Compared to the method of personnel observation experiments, computer simulation techniques have sig­
nificant advantages, as they allow researchers to set individual differences in the model, thereby enhancing the reliability of data
results [29]. Some scholars have already developed dozens of mature evacuation models, with typical simulation micro models for
evacuation primarily including continuous evacuation models and discrete evacuation models [30]. The construction principle of
continuous simulation models is to use kinematic equations and consider various factors related to evacuees and the evacuation space
environment, establishing equation relationships through variable representation. Up to now, widely recognized continuous evacu­
ation simulation models include: the social force model, which integrates multiple variable relationships [31]; the SIMULEX evacu­
ation model, which accommodates multi-level building structures [32]; and the Building Exodus evacuation model, being suitable for
simulating large, complex structures such as metro stations and shopping malls [33]. The discrete simulation model combines Cou­
lomb’s Law, considering individuals as positive charges and their desired destinations as negative charges. Individuals automatically
walk towards their destinations, treating obstacles as positive charges and avoiding them during the evacuation process. The evac­
uation process of individuals can be described as the evacuation individuals being influenced by a magnetic field, based on the
evacuation environment and their own mechanisms, selecting cells to complete actions towards escaping to safety exits [34].
With the continuous development of computer technology, there has been a significant improvement in the accuracy and speed of
metro fire evacuation simulation tools. However, insufficiencies still exist [35]. Therefore, one of the current research directions is to
further enhance the simulation methods in order to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the simulations [36,37]. Additionally, few
researchers explored multi-objective optimization for metro station fire evacuation. One reason is that the difficulty in acquiring the
complex relationship between evacuation objectives and influencing factors, which can vary significantly between different metro
stations. Another reason is that finding an optimal solution that satisfies the evacuation optimization needs of all individuals is
challenging [38]. Currently, only a few researchers have explored the application of data mining and machine learning in metro station
fire evacuation. Machine learning methods can assist researchers in better understanding the relationship between evacuation ob­
jectives and influencing factors during the evacuation process, as well as uncover patterns and regularities hidden within the data [39].
However, there is still a lack of interpretability analysis for machine learning algorithms in predicting evacuation objectives during
metro station fire evacuations.
Overall, current research on fire evacuation modeling and optimization still has several limitations. First, traditional modeling
methods struggle to balance accuracy and computational efficiency, making it difficult to meet the rapid simulation demands of
complex environments like subway stations. Second, most existing evacuation optimization approaches focus on single objectives (e.g.,
shortest time) while neglecting the multi-objective trade-offs (e.g., crowd density, cost) in evacuation processes. Additionally, prior
studies lack in-depth analysis of the nonlinear relationships between various influencing factors and evacuation outcomes in fire
scenarios. Moreover, the poor interpretability of existing models hinders their practical application. Hence, in response to the
aforementioned challenges related to modeling accuracy and evacuation multi-objectives optimization, this study aims to develop an
integrated approach that combines BIM technology and FDS to achieve rapid and precise simulation.

3. Methodology
To effectively simulate and optimize the evacuation of metro station fire scenarios, this study proposes a hybrid method that in­
tegrates BIM, FDS and multi-objectives optimization algorithm. Fig. 1 presents the research framework, which includes three steps of
research activities: (1) carrying out analysis of metro station fire evacuation objectives and influencing factors; (2) simulating different
fire scenarios in metro stations based on BIM and FDS; (3) conducting multi-objectives prediction and optimization of metro station fire
evacuation.
3.1. Evacuation analysis and objectives for metro station
The primary objective of metro station evacuation is to ensure the safety of passengers and minimize casualties [38,40]. Therefore,
evacuation should swiftly, orderly, and safely guide passengers to a safe area, away from fire and smoke, meaning the evacuation time
should be as short as possible [41]. Meanwhile, the evacuation should avoid the occurrence of personnel congestion and stampede
situations. In other words, the evacuation density of people in the evacuation process should be as sparse as possible [42,43]. Addi­
tionally, in order to evaluate the evacuation effect and optimize the renovation, the renovation cost is also included in the evacuation
objective [38,40]. In other words, to optimize metro station fire evacuation, three evacuation objectives, namely evacuation time,
evacuation density and cost, are considered. However, there are contradictions in the above evacuation objectives. For example, the
shorter the evacuation time, it indicates that the crowd will gather more in certain time, resulting in excessive evacuation density.
Thus, how to achieve the balance between evacuation objectives is a main aim of this study.
Implementing a fire evacuation in a metro station requires consideration of numerous factors. Each station possesses unique
characteristics geographically and physically. Thus, there would be some specific factors affecting evaluation process in various metro
station environments. Through literature review, these factors can be roughly divided into three categories, namely passenger factors,
station functionality factors, and guidance under emergency situations [13,38]. Table 1 describes the influencing factors and objec­
tives of fire evacuation in metro stations.
(1) Passenger factors. A particularly striking feature of metro stations is the large number of passengers, and since passengers are
one of the most decisive factors in evacuation events, passenger flow (x1) is set as the key influencing factor in this study [44]. In
addition, the metro station has a diverse distribution of people, including the elderly and children, men and women, and the
walking speed of these people is different. Therefore, in order to achieve the stability and balance of the crowd, the average
walking speed of passengers (x2) is taken as an influencing factor [45,46].
(2) Station functionality factors. The metro stations are large-scale enclosed transportation facilities. In the event of a fire, the
layout of the station, the arrangement of the passages, and the location of the evacuation exits will directly affect the evacuation
efficiency. If the passages of the station are too narrow, there are too few exits, or the layout is chaotic, it will seriously hinder
evacuation, increasing the possibility of people being trapped and casualties [13,47]. Therefore, the number of exits (x3), the
width and length of stairs (x4、 x5 and x6), the length of passageways (x7) and width of passageways (x8) are considered as the
factors affecting the station function.
(3) Guidance under emergency situations. Through the field investigation of the target metro station, obstacles such as billboards,
service desks and cleaning machines were observed. Some studies suggest that the interaction between these obstacles and
passengers may have a great impact on evacuation efficiency [48]. Furthermore, an effective evacuation signage system can

3.2. Evacuation simulation and scenarios design
In order to optimize the evacuation objectives of metro stations under various fire scenarios, this study first established a BIM model
of metro stations, and imported it into the FDS software - Pyrosim for smoke simulation and the fire situation set up. On this basis,
Pathfinder was used to simulate personnel evacuation. In the context of metro stations, the main consideration is the occurrence of fires
caused by passengers carrying suitcases. Research suggests that the fire power caused by suitcases is generally 2 MW. Furthermore,
studies have shown that the power of a fire occurring in the center of a platform is generally 1.5–2.5 MW. Therefore, considering
certain extreme cases, it is ultimately concluded that the range of fire power is 2.0–2.5 MW [53]. The types of combustibles in a fire will
affect the fire development coefficient, thereby directly influencing the speed of fire development. Generally, fire sources can be
classified into four types based on their development speed: extremely fast type, rapid type, medium type and slow type [54]. Due to
certain unpredictable factors, such as passengers carrying flammable items, the fire source power of the metro station as 2.5 MW is
selected, with the metro station fire as a rapidly growing fire and the fire development coefficient as 0.04689 kW/s2. The platform is a
more concentrated place for people waiting for the metro, with larger personnel density. Some studies reveal that the fire spreading on
the platform floor is more dangerous than that spreading in the station hall [55]. To highlight the significant threats that may be faced
after a fire breaks out, therefore the fire source location is set in the center of the platform. Pyrosim simulation mainly includes three
basic processes: model creation, operation solving, and analysis processing. The specific operation process is as follows. Fig. 3 shows
the BIM model of the metro station and the FDS evacuation process.
(1) Identifying targets and import parameters. Importing Revit models of a metro station directly into FDS software. To be specific,
this study mainly outputs the BIM metro station model built by Revit in IFC2x3 Coordination View format, which contains
geometric information, material properties and topological relationships. Autodesk Revit (2023), a conversion tool, was then
utilised to transform the IFC format into DXF 2018 format. This version has been designed to provide robust support for 3D
solids and mesh graphics, thus meeting the import requirements of FDS. In Revit, complex irregular components (e.g., freeform
stairs) were converted by the software into recognizable generic solids (e.g., represented by a combination of extruded solids
and floors). Although some modeling details were sacrificed through this process, it was ensured that geometric information
would be exported completely and accurately as DXF entities. Furthermore, different components (e.g., walls, stairs, corridors)
were assigned by the operator to separate DXF layers, enabling quick selection and uniform assignment of material properties in

3.3. Evacuation multi-objectives prediction and optimization
3.3.1. Prediction model and performance indicators
Although establishing the relationships between fire evacuation objectives in metro stations and the influencing factors on fire
evacuation is challenging due to their complexity, the rapid development of various simulation models and different machine learning
algorithms offers the possibility to solve this problem [38]. Gaussian regression, support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF),
decision trees, and integrated methods (such as AdaBoost and NGBoost) provide ways to construct complex nonlinear relationships
between evacuation objectives and their influencing factors. In this study, several common machine learning prediction algorithms (e.
g. RF, AdaBoost and NGBoost) are used to construct a proxy model between evacuation objectives and their influencing factors, and the
prediction model with higher accuracy is used as the objective function of the final optimization algorithm. In order to ensure the
accuracy of the prediction model, this study adopts Bayesian algorithm (BO) to optimize the machine learning hyperparameters [56].
At the same time, in order to ensure the accuracy of optimization in a later-on stage, root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of

3.3.2. Prediction model interpretability analysis
Due to the “black box” problem in machine learning, the prediction model lacks power of explanation [60]. In order to explain the
contribution of each feature factor in the prediction model to the prediction objectives, SHapley Additive explanation (SHAP) is used
herein to explain the model. It is a global explanation method independent of the model and commonly used to explain any machine
learning model globally [61,62]. This method uses the idea of game theory to measure the influence of features on the model output by
calculating the marginal contribution of each feature’s Shapley value to the model [63]. The Shapley value represents the only fair way
to contribute features. On the average of the calculated marginal contribution of feature i (model outputs with feature i and without
feature i) for all subsets N of S (excluding feature i), the Shapley value i(φi) of specific feature i, the contribution of each feature to the
prediction model, can be calculated [64,65]. The calculation formula is shown in equation (6).

3.3.3. Evacuation optimization
1. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithm based on decomposition (MOEAD) approach
Common multi-objective optimization algorithms such as genetic algorithm (GA), Non-dominant Sorting Genetic algorithm-II
(NSGA-II), particle swarm optimization algorithm, are used widely [25]. The MOEAD decomposes each multi-objective problem
into multiple scalar optimization subproblems. Each subproblem uses only information from neighboring subproblems and evolves a
solution group using crossover and mutation mechanisms, and each generation is less computationally complex than NSGA-II. Some
studies have found that MOEAD has more advantages than NSGA-II in handling Pareto solution sets with more complex shapes [66,
67]. Considering the advantage of MOEAD in solving speed, MOEAD is adopted as multi-objective optimization algorithm in this study.
The general implementation steps of MOEAD are as follows. The pseudocode based on BO-NGBoost-MOEAD algorithm is shown in
Table 2.
(1) The machine learning prediction function is input as the fitness function of MOEAD algorithm. MOEAD explicitly decomposes
multi-objective problems into scalar optimization subproblems while solving these subproblems using a weighted summation
method, converting the subproblems into scalar aggregation functions.
(2) The neighborhood relation between these subproblems is defined according to the distance between their aggregation coeffi­
cient vectors. In MOEAD, each subproblem (i.e., scalar aggregation function) is optimized using only information from
neighboring subproblems and using crossover and mutation mechanisms to evolve the population.
(3) Update the parent population, determine whether the termination condition is met, if so, output the Pareto solution set,
otherwise, continue to run the algorithm.

5. Discussion
5.1. Effect of fire smoke on evacuation
Despite the fact that evacuation time is the primary concern during a metro station fire evacuation, the irreparable harm to human
bodies caused by smoke could not be disregarded. Hence, apart from the evacuation time mandated by the design specification, it is
critical to account for the potential damage inflicted upon the human body by the smoke. This entails the consideration of two critical
time factors: the available safe evacuation time (ASET) and the required safe evacuation time (RSET) [75].
Following the occurrence of a fire, the ASET denotes the period of time within which individuals can be evacuated securely. The
time required to evacuate is contingent upon various factors, such as the magnitude and nature of the fire, the quantity and acces­
sibility of evacuation routes, and the capability of personnel to evacuate. For instance, the fire-produced smoke, high temperature, and
noxious gas will endanger human life, and the smoothness or lack thereof of the evacuation passageway will impact personnel safety
and evacuation velocity. RSET is the duration between obtaining an alarm notification of a fire and the point at which all occupants are
able to evacuate the hazardous area. It comprises three elements: the alarm time, the moment personnel are prepared to evacuate, and
the duration between the commencement of the evacuation and personnel’s complete removal from the hazardous area [76]. The
duration of these intervals is contingent upon the personnel’s readiness and the rapidity of response of the fire alarm system, as well as
the state of the evacuation channels. Notably, ASET must be longer than RSET to assure the safe evacuation of personnel; that is, ASET
> RSET [35]. In order to prevent personal injury from the fire, personnel may only be evacuated safely when the ASET exceeds the
RSET.
To assess the potential harm that smoke may inflict on human beings during the evacuation procedure, the fire scenario presented
herein assumes the following: the fire source is positioned at the platform’s centre, its power is 2.5 MW, and the estimated passenger
flow for the general period is one thousand individuals. Passengers situated at the fire site and on either side will be impacted by the
flames and fumes that propagate directly above the platform’s center. Furthermore, the occupied evacuation channels on both sides
will impede passengers’ ability to evacuate. The simulation results indicate that the flue gas temperature at the left stair attains a
hazardous state of 60 ◦C at 248s (refer to Fig. 15(a)). The CO concentration fails to reach the critical level of 250 ppm within 360s (refer
to Fig. 15(b)). Furthermore, at 69.9s, the visibility reaches a hazardous level of 10m (refer to Fig. 15(c)). It is therefore concluded that
the AEST for the left stair is 69.9 s. At the right stair, the flue gas temperature and CO concentration do not attain the hazardous
thresholds of 60 ◦C and 250 ppm within 360 s, respectively. Additionally, the visibility at 101 s reaches the hazardous level of 10 m.
The smoke and evacuation simulation outcomes are presented in Table 10 through the importation of smoke simulation data at this
moment, subsequent to evacuation simulation in Pathfinder. The REST values for the left and right stairways are as follows: the left
stair has a REST of 62 s, and Fig. 16 illustrates the evacuation situation. The evacuation time for the right stair egress is 75.6 s, as
illustrated in Fig. 16(b). The evacuation efficiencies of the left and right stairs are 88.7 % and 74.9 %, respectively, which are adequate

is viable, as it satisfies the needs of 950 passengers, aligns with the optimization outcomes, and achieves the safe evacuation objective
to the greatest extent possible.

5.3. Evacuation improvement measures
Based on the outcomes of the optimization process, strategies such as directing passenger traffic, enhancing metro station ame­
nities, and fortifying station evacuation signs may be implemented to facilitate fire evacuation in metro stations. Sufficient
enhancement measures are proposed in three areas: passenger flow guidance, metro station design and station facilities improvement.
(1) Ensure a reasonable influx of passengers. Passenger flow should be given due consideration, as it is the principal determinant of
evacuation outcomes [77]. Initially, station personnel are instructed in routine passenger flow guidance exercises in order to
hone their abilities to direct passengers during peak hours and emergency situations. Additionally, distinct guidance strategies
are implemented in accordance with the period of greatest passenger volume. During periods of high demand, for instance,
additional personnel are stationed in strategic locations and around curves to direct passengers as they board and alight the
train in a systematic fashion and to facilitate the flow of individuals in advance. In conclusion, a refined redesign of the station
layout is possible in order to create ample passageways, prevent bottlenecks and congestion, and ensure adequate space [78].
(2) Improve the design of metro stations. As much as feasible, during the design and construction phases of metro stations,
decorative materials that are resistant to combustion should be chosen. The selection of these materials will have an immediate
impact on the type of haze produced and the rate of flame propagation following a fire. Furthermore, it is imperative to
implement suitable mechanical smoke exhaust devices in metro stations to further mitigate the destructive effects of fires.
Mechanical smoke exhaust devices have the capability to efficiently remove smoke from the station, thereby diminishing the
smoke concentration, enhancing the visibility within the station, and facilitating personnel evacuation [79]. Additionally, it is
possible to implement an automated fire alarm system that can promptly identify fires and reduce the time between fire
detection and alarm. This would effectively decrease the necessary safe evacuation time for personnel in metro stations and
enhance the overall fire safety of the facility.
(3) Strengthen the infrastructure of metro stations. Given that passenger evacuation requires the use of the stairs, this study also
considers the stair entrance as a factor in determining evacuation density. Consequently, enhancements to the stair system may
be warranted. To adequately accommodate the station’s passenger traffic requirements, an increase in the quantity of evacu­
ation stairs may be implemented initially. Secondly, consideration must be given to the design and width of the evacuation
stairway. Passenger throughput can be increased and the risk of congestion and pressing decreased by enlarging the stairway
[80]. Furthermore, to facilitate emergency navigation for passengers towards the closest evacuation channel, it is possible to
install conspicuous signs and indicators in close proximity to the station and evacuation stairs [81].

6. Conclusions and future works
To enhance metro station fire evacuations, a hybrid approach is proposed that integrates BIM, FDS, and a multi-objective opti­
mization algorithm founded on BO-NGBoost-MOEAD, which improves the intelligent level of fire evacuation in metro stations. To
commence, a fire simulation was conducted utilising BIM and FDS. The evacuation procedure was forecast using the BO-NGBoost
algorithm, and SHAP was implemented to augment the transparency of the prediction model. Finally, the objective function of the
MOEAD optimization algorithm was the predicted model, which was utilised to renovate metro stations so as to facilitate safe
evacuation in the event of fires. The outcome of this study is the development of decision-making instruments that can be utilised to
optimize evacuation strategies.
The feasibility of this approach was verified by employing a particular metro station in China as an illustrative case. These are the
conclusions reached: (1) The performance of the fire evacuation prediction model for metro stations, which is built upon BO-NGBoost,
surpasses that of RF and AdaBoost. The validation set R2 value for this model exceeds 0.85. According to the findings of the SHAP
interpretability analysis, the passenger flow and number of exits are the two most significant evacuation factors. (3) By renovating
metro stations, the multi-objective optimization based on BO-NGBoost-MOEAD can accomplish efficient fire evacuation. The opti­
mization of three evacuation objectives—ensuring optimum passenger flow—led to the selection of the equilibrium solution. As a
result, the evacuation time, evacuation density, and cost have been enhanced by 31.02 %, 2.70 %, and 51.41 % correspondingly, for a
total improvement of 28.38 %. Finally, measures to promote evacuation optimization, including passenger flow guidance, metro
station design, and evacuation facility enhancement, were proposed. By offering an efficient decision-making instrument for fire
evacuation management in metro stations, the proposed hybrid method can be applied to other scenarios involving metro station
evacuation management. As a result, it contributes to the sustainable development of urban metro operation systems.
However, this investigation is not without its limitations. To begin with, the fire evacuation scenario presented herein is pre­
dominantly generated via simulation using FDS software. On-site verification presents numerous challenges due to practical consid­
erations, and the estimation of renovation costs is susceptible to certain errors. However, the essence of optimization remains
consistent: guaranteeing a secure evacuation during critical situations while accommodating the greatest possible influx of passengers.
Second, while the Steering mode has been modified to accommodate the psychological behaviour of the crowd, it is still incapable of
entirely accounting for the panicked behaviour of passengers during evacuation. Subsequent investigations may contemplate the
implementation of virtual reality (VR) technology in fire evacuation in order to more comprehensively gauge the psychological
conduct of the population throughout the evacuation process [82,83]. Furthermore, to select representative metro station samples
with different layouts and passenger characteristics for additional case studies is meaningful. Finally, constructing a digital twin early
warning system for metro stations in the event of an emergency, including fires and other abrupt occurrences, is a crucial research
endeavour for the sustainable advancement of metro operation systems, in line with the smart city development trend.
